title: The sunnah prayers
hook: regular extra units before and after the obligatory ones

segments.voice: Yesterday, the iqamah: stand now, calm, not a sprint. Before it, there was a space for a prayer. Today, what fills it.

Better than the world and everything in it. That's a big claim to make about two short units of prayer, said quietly in a dark bedroom before the dawn prayer, with the alarm still blinking and nobody watching. Aishah reports the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, saying exactly that about the two units before the dawn prayer, in Sahih Muslim, number 725. Not the obligatory prayer. The small extra one before it. Today, the prayers that sit around the obligatory ones like a frame around a picture.
screen: `BETTER THAN THE WORLD.` → `TWO SHORT UNITS, BEFORE DAWN.` → `A FRAME AROUND A PICTURE.`

segments.voice: The word is rawatib, the regular ones: the voluntary prayers the Prophet ﷺ kept attached to the obligatory prayers, some just before, some just after. Not required, but not random either. In Sahih Muslim, number 728, his wife Umm Habibah reports him saying that whoever prays twelve units a day and night, beyond the obligatory, will have a house built for them in the garden. And Umm Habibah adds that she never stopped praying them after she heard it. Jami at-Tirmidhi, number 415, lays out where those units fall: four before the noon prayer and two after it, two after the sunset prayer, two after the night prayer, and two before dawn. Another companion, Ibn Umar, in Sahih al-Bukhari, number 1180, remembers ten, with two before noon instead of four. The schools follow these reports in slightly different ways, and Shia practice keeps its own pattern of daily voluntary prayers. Among all of them, one pair gets special weight. Aishah says, in Sahih al-Bukhari, number 1169, that the Prophet ﷺ was not more careful about any voluntary prayer than the two before dawn. Why pray what isn't required? One answer is in the word sunnah itself: following how he actually prayed, not only what was demanded. Another is in a hadith in Sunan Abu Dawud, number 864: on the day of reckoning, if the obligatory prayers fall short, the voluntary ones are looked to, to make up what's missing. The frame protects the picture.
screen: `RAWATIB: THE REGULAR ONES.` · `UMM HABIBAH: TWELVE, A HOUSE IN THE GARDEN.` · `THE TWO BEFORE DAWN, KEPT MOST CAREFULLY.` · `THE FRAME PROTECTS THE PICTURE.` · then, large: `BETTER THAN THE WORLD AND ALL IN IT.`

segments.voice: Picture tomorrow morning: the alarm, the dark, the minute before the dawn prayer or before your day begins, and see yourself adding something small and extra there, before the main thing. If you pray, those are the two units before fajr, and you can settle now on praying them; if you don't, choose a two-minute habit to set before the first big task of your day. Then sit quietly with the decision made.
Rawatib. The regular voluntary prayers, before and after the obligatory ones, with the two before dawn kept most carefully of all. Today's word.
Your line: the sunnah around it. Small, extra, and kept, the way Umm Habibah kept hers. Up next: the odd prayer.

howItsDone: Muslims who keep the rawatib pray short voluntary units before or after the obligatory prayers, at home or in the mosque, following the pattern their school teaches, and give particular care to the two units before the dawn prayer.

chat.says: Why pray the extra units before fajr if they aren't even required?
options: They follow how the Prophet prayed, and he guarded those two before dawn most of all.
Because the extra units count toward the obligatory ones and shorten them.
Because the dawn prayer itself is only valid with the extra two first.
chat.meaning: Rawatib aren't required, but they follow how he prayed, and Aishah says he was most careful about the two before dawn.

notes: Hadith numbers and details to confirm: Muslim 725 (Aishah: the two rak'ahs of fajr are better than the world and what is in it); Muslim 728 (Umm Habibah: twelve rak'ahs, a house in Paradise; 'I have not left them since'); Tirmidhi 415 (the distribution of the twelve); Bukhari 1180 (Ibn 'Umar's ten); Bukhari 1169 (Aishah: none more regular than the two before fajr); Abu Dawud 864 (voluntary prayers make up for deficient obligatory ones).
